paras: The killing of Hugh Burns and threatened lynching of John J. Jater took place in Indianapolis, Indiana, on the night of August 28, 1882, when a Kentucky man named in the papers as Jater shot and killed Policeman Hugh Burns, who was trying to arrest him. Jater was caught and jailed, and a widely reprinted telegram said he had "narrowly escaped lynching." No report gave Jater's race or described the threat in racial terms.

The St. Paul Globe's Indianapolis dispatch described Jater as "a drunken tramp" from Taylorsville, Kentucky. A paper at Stanford, Kentucky, which spelled his name Jeter, said he had shot a Black man at Campbellsville, Kentucky, and was "making his way west to escape punishment" when he reached Indianapolis.

According to the Globe's dispatch, Jater was flourishing a revolver and cursing in a crowd when Burns came up, put a hand on his shoulder and said, "You are my prisoner." Jater turned and fired twice, and Burns fell dead. Other versions placed the trouble in a saloon, said Jater had been firing at men who had assaulted him, or said he had picked a quarrel with a stranger while drunk.

Jater then ran but was caught, and the reports agree that he was taken only after resistance or "some difficulty." A condensed telegram added that "the murderer narrowly escaped lynching" before he was jailed, without saying who threatened him or how.
Jater was held in jail, and the Kentucky paper predicted that he would hang "if he gets his deserts." No report of an inquest, indictment or trial appears in the coverage found.

The story ran in white papers from Minnesota and Wisconsin to Tennessee, Alabama and Kentucky between August 30 and early September 1882, mostly as a single paragraph in roundups of telegraphic news. The Globe headed its dispatch "He Wasn't His Prisoner, Though," while the condensed-telegram version that mentioned lynching ran in the Milan Exchange and the Huntsville Gazette on September 2. The Watertown Republican later reduced the story to one line in a crime roundup, and the papers spelled the surname three ways: Jater, Joter and Jeter.

Accounts differ on how Burns was hit: the Globe said one ball passed through his shoulder, while the Kentucky paper said it passed through his heart. Only the condensed telegram mentioned a lynching threat; the earlier Indianapolis dispatch reported simply that Jater was caught and jailed.

reader.title: Killing of Hugh Burns and threatened lynching of John J. Jater
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
bases: The only collective violence reported is that the accused 'narrowly escaped lynching' after shooting a policeman (A4, A5); the core event is a shooting of an officer by an individual (A1, A2, A3), and no report gives the accused's race.
Jater was not killed; he was jailed (A1, A3, A4). A condensed telegram says only that he 'narrowly escaped lynching', without describing a mob, its size or its acts (A4).

Several independent reports agree that Hugh Burns was shot dead by Jater while trying to arrest him and that Jater was jailed (A1, A2, A3, A4); the lynching threat rests on a single condensed-telegram paragraph (A4, reprinted A5).

accounts.gist: Jater, drunk, was flourishing a revolver and cursing in a crowd; when Burns put a hand on his shoulder and said 'You are my prisoner,' Jater shot him twice and ran, but was caught and jailed.

accounts.label: Watertown Republican brief
accounts.gist: Joter had been firing his revolver at men who had assaulted him when the officer interfered and was killed.

accounts.label: Kentucky report
accounts.gist: Jeter, fleeing west after shooting a Black man in Campbellsville, got drunk, picked a quarrel with a stranger and shot Burns through the heart; he was arrested after some difficulty.

accounts.label: Condensed telegram
accounts.gist: Burns was shot while quelling a saloon disturbance; Jater narrowly escaped lynching and was jailed after a stubborn resistance.

framing.detail: Most papers carried the story as a single paragraph in roundups of telegraphic news, calling Jater 'the murderer' and noting the lynching threat without comment.
The St. Paul Globe headed its dispatch 'He Wasn't His Prisoner, Though.' and called Jater a 'drunken tramp'.
The Stanford, Ky., paper called Jeter 'a very desperate character' who 'will hang' if he got his deserts.
